name: Columbus
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Columbus, OH | Genstone
metaDescription: Investor renovations in Columbus, OH: free pre-offer rehab reviews, written scopes and draws for flips, BRRRR, rentals, doubles, 203(k) and REO homes.
intro:
Columbus is the rare Ohio market where an investor can run almost any renovation strategy within a short drive. Brick worker cottages in German Village and Merion Village, frame doubles in Old North Columbus and Weinland Park, bungalows and Cape Cods in Clintonville and the Hilltop, and post-war ranches across Northland and Westgate all trade here, and each one hides a different set of scope risks.

Genstone Construction renovates for investors, lenders and servicers in Columbus by coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors under one designated field manager, with estimating, permitting support and draw documentation run from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. Before you commit capital, our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the repairs, pressure-tests your after-repair value and tells you whether the deal still works at your offer. After closing you get a written scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, no upfront payment, draws released only against finished work, and a one-year workmanship warranty.
housingStock:
Columbus grew in layers, and you can usually date a house's problems by its street. The oldest stock sits just south of downtown in German Village and Merion Village, where narrow brick cottages from the 1800s stand on shallow brick or rubble foundations with tight lot lines and almost no room for staging. Italian Village, Victorian Village and Olde Towne East carry larger Victorian and Queen Anne houses, many with balloon framing, plaster on wood lath and built-in box gutters that have been patched for generations.

The streetcar era filled the Near East Side, Linden, Franklinton, the Hilltop and the University District with frame American Foursquares, gable-front houses and side-by-side doubles. These are the workhorses of the local rental market. Expect knob-and-tube wiring buried behind later circuits, galvanized supply piping, cast-iron stacks feeding clay sewer laterals, and lead paint on nearly every original surface. Basements are commonly fieldstone or brick with low headroom and seepage at the floor joint.

Clintonville, Beechwold and the South Side added Craftsman bungalows, Tudors and brick Cape Cods between the World Wars. Construction quality there is generally solid, but half-story bedrooms with knee walls tend to be thinly insulated and hot in July.

After 1945 the city annexed aggressively, which is why Northland, Westgate and Eastmoor are full of ranches, split-levels and crawlspace homes. Those can hide asbestos in floor tile, duct wrap and textured ceilings, and many still have original electrical panels and aluminum windows.

For a rehab, the era decides where the budget is soft. Older brick stock eats money in masonry, drainage and electrical. Frame doubles need fire separation and split utilities to perform as rentals. Post-war ranches look inexpensive until the layout, ductwork and abatement are priced honestly.

commonIssues.title: Live knob-and-tube behind newer outlets
commonIssues.body: Pre-1930 houses in Linden, the Hilltop, Franklinton and the University District often still carry energized knob-and-tube circuits that a previous owner extended with modern outlets. Insurers and rental lenders frequently refuse it, and buyers' inspectors flag it immediately. We price a full rewire with a new service rather than piecemeal fixes, and we sequence it with plaster repair and lead-safe work so the walls are opened once instead of three times.

commonIssues.title: Seeping basements and tired sewer laterals
commonIssues.body: Fieldstone and brick basements sitting in central Ohio's clay till seep wherever downspouts dump at the wall. Clay laterals under older streets collect roots and offset joints. Camera the lateral before you make an offer. In neighborhoods covered by Blueprint Columbus, the city has been lining laterals and redirecting downspouts, so ask whether the property already received that work before you budget for it yourself.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint on almost every original surface
commonIssues.body: Nearly all of the urban core was built long before 1978, so window sashes, porch columns, trim and stair parts should be treated as lead-bearing until tested. That matters for crew practices under the EPA's lead-safe renovation rules and for rentals housing young children. Replacing friction surfaces like old sashes and door jambs often costs less over a hold than repeatedly scraping and repainting them.

commonIssues.title: Doubles that share everything
commonIssues.body: Many Columbus doubles were converted or built with one water service, a shared attic, a party wall with no real fire separation and sometimes a single gas meter. They rent fine until a tenant dispute over utilities or a fire inspection forces the issue. Separating meters, closing the attic at the party wall and adding fire-rated assemblies is often what turns a cheap double into a financeable one.

commonIssues.title: Asbestos and dated mechanicals in post-war ranches
commonIssues.body: Ranches and split-levels in Northland, Westgate and Eastmoor were built during the peak years for asbestos floor tile, duct tape wrap and popcorn ceilings. Disturbing them without testing exposes you to cleanup costs and delays. The same houses tend to have original furnaces, undersized ductwork laid out for a closed floor plan and aluminum windows, so an open-concept flip usually needs mechanical redesign, not just new equipment.

investorMarket:
Columbus rewards investors who match the strategy to the neighborhood rather than chasing one playbook citywide.

Flips work best where buyers already compete: Clintonville, Old North Columbus, Merion Village, Schumacher Place and the edges of German Village and Italian Village. Those buyers know the comps, expect finished basements to be dry and will notice a cheap kitchen. Margins come from correctly scoping the old systems, not from cutting finishes.

Buy-and-hold investors concentrate on the Hilltop, Linden, the South Side, Driving Park and parts of Northland, where entry prices are lower and the renter pool is deep. Those houses suit BRRRR if the scope stays disciplined and the refinance comps hold up on the same street.

Small multifamily is a Columbus specialty. Side-by-side doubles in Old North, Weinland Park and Olde Towne East, plus converted houses near Ohio State, give investors two incomes on one lot, though student-area units take harder wear and turn on a fixed calendar.

REO and bank-owned inventory appears throughout the older eastern and western neighborhoods and in post-war subdivisions where a vacant winter can do real damage. FHA 203(k) buyers tend to target Clintonville, Linden and South Side bungalows that need work but have good bones, often with an agent who has seen a conventional loan fall apart over condition.

Across every strategy, the steady expansion of the metro keeps demand broad, but it also means plenty of competition. Accurate pre-offer pricing is where most deals are won or lost.
permits:
Inside city limits, permits come from the City of Columbus Department of Building and Zoning Services. One-, two- and three-family houses fall under the Residential Code of Ohio, while a four-unit building moves into the Ohio Building Code and is treated as commercial work. Structural changes, new or relocated plumbing, electrical service upgrades, HVAC replacement, egress windows in basement bedrooms, decks and roofing tear-offs that touch sheathing generally need permits and inspections. Cosmetic work such as paint, flooring and cabinet swaps usually does not.

Exterior changes in German Village, Italian Village, Victorian Village and other designated districts must be approved by the relevant architectural review commission before work starts, which affects windows, doors, roofing material, porches and siding. Build that review into the schedule rather than discovering it after materials are ordered.

Electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors hold state licenses through the Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board, and Columbus also requires contractors to be registered with the city. If you plan to rent the house, Columbus requires residential rental properties to be registered with the Franklin County Auditor. Suburbs such as Whitehall, Reynoldsburg and Grove City run their own building departments with their own fees and inspection habits.
climate:
Central Ohio sits in a humid continental pattern with real winters and sticky summers, and both affect rehab scope. Frequent freeze-thaw swings are hard on brick, mortar joints, concrete steps and older porch footings, so tuckpointing and flatwork are best scheduled when overnight temperatures stay above freezing.

Spring brings the heaviest rains of the year, and that is when clay-soil basements reveal themselves. If you buy in winter, assume a dry-looking basement has not been tested and budget for grading, downspout extensions or interior drainage accordingly.

Summers are humid enough that renters and buyers expect central air. Older houses with knee-wall bedrooms or no ductwork may need ductless systems or a carefully routed duct run. Ice storms and wind events occasionally take down limbs and gutters. Vacant houses left unheated over a cold snap are the most common source of burst pipes in this market.

faqs.q: Do you have a Columbus office?
faqs.a: No. Genstone Construction is headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and we run Columbus projects by coordinating vetted, licensed and insured local contractors. Estimating, scope writing, draw management and documentation are handled by our team, and each project has a designated field manager from start to finish. You see progress photos, milestones and draw requests without needing to be on site, which is why many of our Columbus clients are out-of-state investors and lenders.

faqs.q: Can you look at a Columbus house before I make an offer?
faqs.a: Yes. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built for that moment. We estimate the repair cost, check your after-repair value assumptions against the condition and finish level the comps require, and tell you plainly whether the numbers support your offer. For Columbus houses, that review usually focuses on electrical era, basement water, sewer lateral condition, lead paint and whether a historic commission will affect exterior work.

faqs.q: How do payments work on a Columbus renovation?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. The estimate includes a draw schedule tied to defined milestones, and each draw is released only after that work is complete and documented. Dumpster and debris removal are already in the estimate rather than billed later. Final payment comes after completion and your approval. If you finance through Genstone Financial or another lender, the draw schedule is written so it lines up with how the lender inspects and releases funds.

faqs.q: Do you handle Columbus suburbs too?
faqs.a: Yes. We work in Whitehall, Reynoldsburg, Grove City, Westerville, Hilliard, Gahanna, Bexley, Upper Arlington and other Franklin County communities. Each suburb has its own building department and some have their own inspection quirks, so the scope and schedule are written for the specific municipality rather than assuming Columbus rules apply. Housing in those suburbs runs from 1920s brick in Bexley to post-war ranches in Whitehall, and the estimate reflects that.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Columbus, OH | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip renovations in Columbus, OH: pre-offer rehab reviews, finishes matched to Clintonville and Merion Village comps, and draws tied to finished work.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Columbus
fix-flip.intro: A Columbus flip is won on the scope sheet before demolition starts. The buyers paying top dollar in Clintonville, Old North and Merion Village are educated, often arriving with a sharp inspector, and they discount hard for old wiring, a damp basement or a kitchen that looks rushed. Genstone Construction scopes and manages flips for investors here with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, a written estimate that often shows more than one finish level against the after-repair value, and a designated field manager who keeps local crews moving. Draws are tied to completed work, debris removal is included, and you pay nothing up front. The goal is a house that sells on the first round of showings, not one that needs a price cut after the inspection report comes back.

sections.h2: Finishing to the comp on each Columbus street
sections.body:
Finish level in Columbus varies more by block than many out-of-town investors expect. A brick cottage in Merion Village or Schumacher Place competes with houses that have quartz counters, refinished original floors and a restored front facade, so builder-grade laminate will cost you more on the sale than it saved on the budget. A Hilltop or Linden flip, on the other hand, sells to first-time buyers and FHA borrowers who care more about a new roof, a newer furnace and a clean inspection than about tile choices.

We price at least two finish packages when the comps are mixed, and we tie each one to the after-repair value it supports. In Clintonville, that often means keeping the bungalow character, opening the kitchen only where the structure allows it, and spending on the bathroom buyers see first. In Old North, it may mean finishing the attic into a usable bedroom so the house lines up with three-bedroom comps.

The point is not to build the nicest house on the street. It is to build the house the street's recent sales say a buyer will pay for, without leaving money on the table.

sections.h2: Where Columbus flip budgets usually break
sections.body:
The overruns we see in this market rarely come from cabinets. They come from what is behind the plaster and under the slab. Pre-1930 houses commonly hide knob-and-tube on circuits that look modern at the outlet, and a buyer's inspector will find it. Clay sewer laterals under older streets crack and collect roots, and a scope that skipped the camera inspection ends up paying for excavation mid-project. Fieldstone basement walls in the South Side and Near East Side need repointing, drainage and sometimes interior waterproofing before anyone finishes them.

In German Village and Italian Village, the commission review can change your window and door budget, since replacement units often need to match the historic profile. Post-war ranches in Northland and Westgate bring their own surprises: asbestos floor tile under carpet and ductwork that cannot serve an open plan.

Our pre-offer estimate calls these out with line items instead of a contingency guess. If the lateral, panel or foundation is suspect, we tell you what it likely needs and how it changes your maximum offer before you sign anything.

sections.h2: Controlling time and carrying cost on a Columbus flip
sections.body:
Every month a flip sits unfinished costs interest, insurance, utilities and taxes, so sequencing matters as much as pricing. In Columbus, the slow steps tend to be permit review for structural or service work, historic district approvals where they apply, and scheduling inspections around trade crews.

We submit permit packages early, order long-lead items such as windows and custom-size doors as soon as the scope is final, and stack trades so rough-in inspections happen together rather than one at a time. Exterior masonry and concrete get scheduled for workable weather, while interior trades carry the project through the colder months.

You can follow milestones, photos and draw requests without driving to the site, and your field manager flags anything that would change the timeline or budget before it happens. When the work is done, the house is cleaned, the dumpster is gone and the punch list is closed so your agent can list it immediately. Final payment comes only after you approve the finished project.

faqs.q: Which Columbus neighborhoods work best for flips?
faqs.a: Clintonville, Old North Columbus, Merion Village, Schumacher Place and the edges of Italian Village draw buyers who pay for finished work, so flips there can support a fuller scope. Hilltop, Linden and the South Side sell to more price-sensitive buyers, where a tight scope focused on systems and curb appeal tends to perform better. The right answer depends on the specific street's recent sales, which is what our pre-offer review checks.

faqs.q: Do flips in German Village need special approval?
faqs.a: Exterior changes in German Village go through the German Village Commission before work begins, and that covers items like windows, doors, roofing, porches and masonry. Interior renovation generally is not subject to that review. We account for the approval step in the schedule and price replacement windows and doors to the profiles the commission typically expects, so you are not surprised by a denial after materials are ordered.

faqs.q: Can I get more than one finish level priced on a Columbus flip?
faqs.a: Yes. When comps are mixed or a house sits between two price bands, our estimate often shows multiple plans with different finish levels and the after-repair value each one is aimed at. That lets you decide whether a fuller kitchen and bath package is worth it on that block or whether a tighter scope gets you to a sale with less capital at risk.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Columbus, OH | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in Columbus, OH built for the refinance appraisal and rental wear: Hilltop, Linden and South Side houses scoped, drawn and documented for lenders.
brrrr.intro: The BRRRR math in Columbus usually depends on buying an older house on the Hilltop, in Linden, on the South Side or in Driving Park, renovating it enough to appraise well, and then holding it through years of tenant turnover. Both halves of that have to be true. A cosmetic rehab that skips the electrical or the sewer lateral will trip up the appraiser or the refinance lender, and a polished flip-grade finish will wear badly under renters. Genstone Construction scopes BRRRR projects here with the refinance appraisal and the long hold in mind, using vetted local contractors, a designated field manager and draw documentation your lender can follow. Genstone Financial also offers DSCR rental loans if you want the takeout and the renovation coordinated under one roof.

sections.h2: Renovating to the Columbus refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers working the Hilltop, Linden and South Side lean on recent renovated sales nearby, and those comps are not always plentiful on every block. That makes condition and functional items more important than design choices. A full bathroom count that matches the comps, a finished bedroom with legal egress, updated electrical, a newer roof and a functioning central HVAC system move a Columbus appraisal far more than an upgraded backsplash.

We start BRRRR projects by reviewing the comps your lender is likely to use and building the scope backward from them. If adding a half bath in a Foursquare's back hall or turning an attic into a permitted bedroom puts the house into a stronger comp set, we price it and show you the tradeoff. If the comps cap the value regardless of finish, we keep the money in systems.

Documentation matters at refinance too. Permits closed, inspection records, a photo trail and a clear scope of work help an appraiser and an underwriter understand what changed, especially on a house that looked rough at purchase.

sections.h2: Rental-grade materials for older Columbus houses
sections.body:
A BRRRR property in Columbus may see a long run of tenants, so finishes have to be chosen for the hold. We use luxury vinyl plank over leveled subfloors instead of carpet in living areas, semi-gloss paint in kitchens and baths, solid-surface or quartz tops that survive abuse, and fixtures with parts you can still buy years from now.

Older houses here need a few extra calls. Plaster walls are durable but crack along old movement lines, so we decide room by room whether to skim, patch or replace with drywall. Original wood windows in pre-1978 homes are a lead hazard at the friction points and a heat-loss problem in January, and replacing them often pays off in fewer complaints and lower utility exposure. Clay-soil basements get proper grading and downspout extensions so the furnace and water heater are not sitting in water.

The aim is a house that refinances well and then quietly produces rent, without a stream of work orders that erodes the return.

sections.h2: Draws, documentation and timing for the Columbus BRRRR cycle
sections.body:
BRRRR depends on recycling capital, so the speed of the rehab and the cleanliness of the paperwork both affect your next purchase. Genstone does not take payment up front. Draws are tied to completed milestones, each backed by photos and progress notes, and that structure fits the way most hard money and construction lenders release funds.

In Columbus, permit timing through the Department of Building and Zoning Services and inspection scheduling are the usual pacing items, along with weather windows for roofing and masonry. We order long-lead materials early and group inspections where possible to avoid idle days.

If you intend to rent the house inside Columbus, plan on registering it with the Franklin County Auditor as a rental. When the work is complete, you receive closeout documentation for your refinance file, and the one-year workmanship warranty covers our work during the early part of the hold, separate from tenant damage and normal wear.

faqs.q: Which Columbus areas work for BRRRR?
faqs.a: Investors most often run BRRRR on the Hilltop, in Linden, on the South Side, in Driving Park and in parts of Northland, where purchase prices leave room for a renovation and the renter pool is deep. Success depends on whether nearby renovated sales support the refinance value, so we look at the specific street's comps during the free pre-offer review before you commit to a scope or a price.

faqs.q: What renovations raise a Columbus refinance appraisal the most?
faqs.a: Functional improvements tend to matter more than design upgrades. Adding a bathroom where the comps have one more, creating a legal bedroom with proper egress, replacing a failing roof, updating the electrical service and installing central air usually move value. Cosmetic upgrades beyond what the comps show rarely pay back at appraisal, so we keep finishes durable and spend where the appraiser will give credit.

faqs.q: Can Genstone coordinate the refinance loan as well?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, offers DSCR rental loans and fix-and-flip loans, so you can coordinate the renovation and the takeout loan with one group if you choose. You are free to use any lender you prefer. Either way, our draw schedule and documentation are written so a lender can follow the work and release funds without confusion.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Columbus, OH | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovations in Columbus, OH: durable, tenant-ready scopes for Hilltop, Linden and Northland homes, with photo-documented draws and turns.
rental-renovation.intro: Rental owners in Columbus range from local landlords with a handful of Hilltop houses to funds holding hundreds of homes across Franklin County. The renovation question is the same at every size: what scope makes this house tenant-ready, keeps it that way through several turnovers and fits the rent it will actually command. Genstone Construction renovates single-family rentals here to consistent portfolio standards, coordinating licensed local trades under a designated field manager and documenting every draw. For owners with ongoing turns, Genstone Field Services handles inspections, make-ready work and occupied maintenance, so the initial renovation and the years that follow can be managed by people who already know the house and its history.

sections.h2: Setting a portfolio standard for Columbus rentals
sections.body:
Owners with more than a few Columbus rentals benefit from a written standard: one flooring product, one paint color family, specified faucets and fixtures, a defined appliance package and a list of required system upgrades. That standard makes estimates comparable, speeds up turns and lets maintenance techs stock fewer parts.

We adapt the standard to the city's housing eras rather than forcing one spec on everything. A post-war ranch in Northland can take a straightforward package. A 1910s Foursquare on the Hilltop may need plaster repair instead of drywall, a dedicated circuit plan because the original wiring cannot carry modern loads, and window replacement because the old sashes are a lead hazard. A Clintonville bungalow rented to professionals may justify a slightly higher kitchen finish to hold its rent tier.

The scope document lists each item by room with labor and materials, so your asset manager can approve, defer or swap items before work begins, and you can compare houses across the portfolio on the same terms.

sections.h2: Building for turnover in older Columbus housing
sections.body:
The materials that survive tenants are not always the ones that photograph well, and older Columbus houses add their own stresses. We favor waterproof plank flooring with transitions that will not lift, solid-core doors at bedrooms and baths, metal or high-impact trim where furniture tends to hit, and paint that can be touched up without a full room repaint.

Basements deserve attention because many tenants use them for storage and laundry. Grading, downspout extensions and sealed penetrations keep spring rains in clay soil from turning into mold complaints. Furnaces and water heaters get raised or protected where seepage is likely. Kitchens get a range hood that vents outside when the route exists, which cuts down on grease and moisture problems.

For houses near Ohio State rented to students, expect harder use and a predictable summer turnover window. We plan those renovations around the academic calendar and specify tougher finishes for shared spaces.

sections.h2: Rental registration, lead safety and code readiness in Columbus
sections.body:
Columbus requires residential rental properties to be registered with the Franklin County Auditor, and rentals within city limits remain subject to code enforcement on complaint. A renovation is the cheapest moment to bring a house into line with what an inspector or a tenant would flag later: working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, secured handrails, egress from sleeping rooms, GFCI protection near water and a safe electrical panel.

Because nearly all of the city's older rental stock predates 1978, we treat original paint as lead-bearing and plan work to EPA lead-safe practices. Replacing worn windows, stabilizing porch paint and addressing friction surfaces reduce the chance of a lead hazard showing up once a family with young children moves in.

Each project closes with photos, a completed scope checklist and records of permits and inspections. Those files help with insurance, financing, future dispositions and resolving any tenant dispute about the condition of the unit at move-in.

faqs.q: Do you handle rental turns in Columbus after the initial renovation?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services handles turn and make-ready work, inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance. Many owners use Genstone Construction for the initial renovation and Field Services for turns, so the same records, standards and photo history follow the house. That continuity helps when you are deciding whether a recurring issue, such as basement moisture, needs a capital fix rather than another repair.

faqs.q: Do Columbus rentals need to be registered?
faqs.a: Yes. Columbus requires residential rental properties to be registered with the Franklin County Auditor. Registration is the owner's responsibility, not the contractor's, but we plan the renovation so the house is ready for occupancy and for any code inspection that follows a tenant complaint. Suburbs outside the city have their own rules, which we check for the specific municipality. If you are buying a house that a previous owner rented, confirm whether the registration is current before your first lease.

faqs.q: What flooring holds up best in Columbus rentals?
faqs.a: For most single-family rentals here, waterproof luxury vinyl plank over a properly leveled subfloor is the practical choice for living areas, kitchens and baths. Older Columbus houses often have uneven floors that need leveling or sistered joists first. Carpet, if used at all, is usually limited to bedrooms in higher-rent houses where tenants expect it. In damp basements we avoid carpet entirely and use a plank rated for below-grade installation.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2-4 Unit Renovation in Columbus, OH | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Duplex and 2-4 unit renovations in Columbus, OH: side-by-side doubles in Old North and Weinland Park, split utilities, fire separation and occupied phasing.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovations in Columbus
multifamily-renovation.intro: The signature small rental building in Columbus is the side-by-side double: two attached units under one roof, each with its own front door and stairs, lining streets in Old North Columbus, Weinland Park, the University District, Olde Towne East and parts of the South Side. Add up-and-down conversions and the occasional brick fourplex, and the city has a deep supply of 2–4 unit buildings. Renovating them is different from renovating a single-family house. Shared systems, fire separation, utility metering and tenants who may still be living there all shape the scope. Genstone Construction plans and manages Columbus multifamily renovations with phasing, separate unit budgets and draw documentation, coordinating licensed local contractors under one field manager.

sections.h2: What makes a Columbus double different
sections.body:
Columbus doubles look simple from the street but often hide decades of shortcuts inside. Many share one water service, a common attic with no separation at the party wall and a basement that was never divided. Some were converted from single-family houses with one electrical service that was later split, sometimes informally. Each of those conditions affects safety, tenant billing and whether a lender will treat the building as two clean units.

A sound renovation usually separates utilities so each unit pays its own gas and electric, extends fire-rated separation through the attic and basement, and checks that each side has its own heating system and water heater. Stairs, handrails and porch structures need attention because double porches take heavy use and weather.

Near Ohio State, doubles are frequently rented by the bedroom, which raises questions about occupancy, egress windows in every sleeping room and the number of smoke alarms. We scope those buildings with student wear in mind and schedule the work around the summer turnover window.

sections.h2: Phasing work with tenants in place
sections.body:
Many Columbus small multifamily purchases come with at least one occupied unit. Vacating everything is not always possible or desirable, so we plan renovations that keep one side producing income while the other is opened up.

That means a phased scope: the vacant unit gets the full interior renovation first, while shared work such as roofing, masonry, gutters, sewer lateral replacement and electrical service upgrades is scheduled with advance notice to occupants and with utilities kept on for them. When the first unit is finished and leased, the second can be renovated, sometimes by moving the existing tenant across.

Shared-system work is where coordination counts. Replacing a lateral, separating gas meters or upgrading a service will interrupt utilities for a period, and the utility companies set part of that schedule. Your field manager handles notices, keeps work hours reasonable and documents the condition of the occupied unit before and after, which protects you if a tenant later disputes damage.

sections.h2: Code, permits and financing for 2–4 units in Columbus
sections.body:
Under Ohio's codes, one-, two- and three-family buildings are covered by the Residential Code of Ohio, while a four-unit building is treated under the Ohio Building Code as commercial construction. In practice that means a fourplex renovation in Columbus can involve different plan review, fire separation requirements and inspection expectations than a double, and the scope should be written for the right code from the start.

Permits for structural work, service upgrades, new plumbing and mechanical replacement come through the City of Columbus Department of Building and Zoning Services. Buildings in the Italian Village, Victorian Village or Old Town East districts also need exterior approvals from the local commission.

Lenders underwriting small multifamily, including DSCR lenders such as Genstone Financial, look closely at whether units are truly separate and safe. Clean separations, closed permits and documentation of what was done make the building easier to finance, insure and eventually sell.

faqs.q: Should I separate utilities when renovating a Columbus double?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Separate gas and electric meters let each tenant pay their own bills, reduce disputes and make the building easier to underwrite. The cost and feasibility depend on the existing service, the gas line layout and utility company requirements. We assess this during the pre-offer review so the separation cost is in your numbers before you buy.

faqs.q: Can you renovate one side of a double while the other is rented?
faqs.a: Yes. Phasing is common in Columbus. The vacant side is fully renovated while shared exterior and system work is scheduled with notice to the occupied side. Utilities stay on for the tenant except during short, planned interruptions, and we document the occupied unit's condition before work begins and after it finishes. Once the first side is leased, the second side can follow, sometimes by moving the existing tenant into the finished unit.

faqs.q: Is a Columbus fourplex renovated differently than a duplex?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A four-unit building falls under the Ohio Building Code rather than the Residential Code of Ohio, which can change plan review, fire separation and inspection requirements. We write the scope for the correct code from the start, so the permit process and the budget reflect the building you actually own. That distinction also matters when you compare purchase prices, because a fourplex that needs commercial-level fire separation can carry a very different renovation cost than a double on the same street.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Columbus, OH | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for Columbus, OH buyers and agents: Limited and Standard 203(k) bids for Clintonville, Linden and South Side fixer-uppers.
fha-203k.intro: In Columbus, an FHA 203(k) loan often makes the difference for a buyer who loves a Clintonville bungalow, a Linden Foursquare or a South Side brick cottage that will not pass a conventional appraisal or an FHA condition review as-is. The loan rolls the purchase and renovation into one mortgage, but it only works when the contractor understands the paperwork, the draw structure and the timeline lenders expect. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor. We work with Columbus buyers, their agents, loan officers and 203(k) consultants to produce a detailed, itemized bid, schedule the work around the loan's draw process and coordinate vetted local trades through completion. That makes us a practical partner for agents who have watched a fixer-upper sale fall through over condition.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard 203(k) for a Columbus house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs and improvements, with a $5,000 minimum and a cap of $75,000 in repair costs. It fits many Columbus houses where the bones are sound but the systems and finishes are tired: a Clintonville bungalow that needs a new roof, furnace, electrical panel and kitchen, or a post-war ranch in Northland that needs windows, flooring and a bath.

The Standard 203(k) is for larger or structural work and requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant. It is often the better fit for older Near East Side, Linden and Hilltop houses where foundation repair, a full rewire from knob-and-tube, a new sewer lateral, a rebuilt porch or a reconfigured floor plan is part of the scope.

We help buyers and agents decide early which path fits. If the house hides structural issues, trying to squeeze it into a Limited loan usually leads to change orders the loan cannot absorb. Our pre-offer review flags those conditions before the buyer is committed.

sections.h2: Columbus houses that fit the 203(k) well
sections.body:
The program works best on houses where the buyer gains real value by fixing what scared off conventional buyers. In Columbus, that often means pre-war houses in Linden, the South Side, Driving Park and the Hilltop with outdated electrical, original windows, failing roofs and dated kitchens. It also includes Clintonville and Beechwold bungalows that sell at a discount because they need significant system work.

Some properties are poor candidates. Houses with serious foundation movement, major water infiltration or long-vacant condition can still be done under a Standard 203(k), but the scope, consultant involvement and contingency need to be honest from the start. Brick cottages in German Village can qualify too, though exterior work must clear the commission, which affects the timeline the lender is expecting.

Because nearly all of these houses predate 1978, lead-safe work practices apply to the renovation, and painted surfaces that will be disturbed need to be planned for. We account for that in the bid rather than treating it as a surprise.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws on a Columbus 203(k)
sections.body:
A 203(k) bid has to be detailed and itemized, matching the consultant's work write-up on a Standard loan and the lender's requirements on a Limited one. We prepare bids that list each item with labor and materials so the lender and consultant can reconcile them quickly. Vague line items are the most common cause of delay.

After closing, funds are held in an escrow and released in draws as work is completed and inspected. The program's $15,000 inspection threshold and the consultant's draw inspections on Standard loans set the rhythm. Our draw requests are tied to completed work with photos, which keeps releases moving and the project on track.

Permits are pulled through the City of Columbus Department of Building and Zoning Services or the relevant suburban department. The buyer often needs to move in on a set schedule, so we sequence the work to get kitchens, baths and mechanical systems functioning as early as the scope allows.

faqs.q: Is Genstone an FHA 203(k) approved contractor in Columbus?
faqs.a: Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor and works with buyers, agents, loan officers and 203(k) consultants in Columbus. We provide itemized bids in the format lenders expect, coordinate vetted local trades, pull permits and submit draw requests tied to completed, documented work. Each project has a designated field manager, so the buyer, agent and loan officer have one point of contact for schedule and draw questions from closing until the final inspection.

faqs.q: Which Columbus homes need a Standard 203(k) instead of a Limited one?
faqs.a: Houses needing structural repairs, foundation work, room additions or reconfiguration, or repairs beyond the $75,000 Limited cap usually require a Standard 203(k) with a HUD-approved consultant. In Columbus, that often includes older Linden, Hilltop and Near East Side houses with failing foundations, full knob-and-tube rewires and major sewer lateral replacement. If you are unsure, our pre-offer review identifies the structural items early so the loan type is chosen correctly the first time.

faqs.q: Can a Columbus agent bring you in before the buyer makes an offer?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the best time. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review gives the agent and buyer a realistic repair estimate, flags structural or system issues that affect which 203(k) path fits and helps the buyer offer with confidence. It also helps the loan officer plan the loan amount before the contract is signed. For agents, that early estimate can keep a deal alive that would otherwise stall when the inspection report arrives.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Columbus, OH | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned property renovations in Columbus, OH for servicers, banks, REITs and GSEs: freeze damage, mold, code violations and occupancy-ready repairs.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovations in Columbus
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned houses in Columbus tend to share a story: months or years of vacancy, at least one winter without reliable heat, and an exterior that has drawn the attention of code enforcement. Getting them back to marketable or rentable condition takes a contractor that understands servicer requirements, documents everything and moves quickly to stop further loss. Genstone Construction renovates REO and bank-owned properties for mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and we are a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. In Columbus, we coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors under a designated field manager, with Genstone Field Services available for preservation, inspections and code compliance before and after the renovation.

sections.h2: What a vacant Columbus winter does to a house
sections.body:
Central Ohio winters are cold enough that an unheated, poorly winterized house will freeze. Burst supply lines, split water heaters, cracked toilet tanks and frozen traps are common in REO inventory here, and the water that follows the thaw soaks plaster ceilings, subfloors and finished basements. If the gas was shut off by the utility, the furnace may also have been damaged or stripped.

Mold follows quickly in closed-up houses with clay-soil basements and roof leaks. Older Hilltop, Linden and Near East Side houses with fieldstone foundations are especially prone to standing water after spring rains if sump pumps or downspouts have failed.

We begin with a condition assessment that separates water-damaged materials from salvageable ones, identifies active leaks and documents everything for the asset manager. Our scope addresses stabilization first: stopping water, drying out, removing contaminated materials and securing the structure. Then we move into the renovation that the disposition or rental strategy calls for.

sections.h2: Vandalism, scrapping and code enforcement in Columbus
sections.body:
Vacant houses in some Columbus neighborhoods attract break-ins and metal theft. Copper supply lines, HVAC condensers, water heaters and even aluminum downspouts are targets, and a stripped house can look intact from the street. We assume nothing until the house has been walked and photographed.

Code enforcement is the other pressure. City of Columbus code officers cite vacant houses for tall grass, accumulated debris, open or broken windows, peeling paint and deteriorated porches and roofs. A property that has collected orders needs those addressed promptly to avoid fines and escalation.

Our REO scopes often begin with a securing and cleanup phase that resolves outstanding violations: board-up or glazing, debris removal, exterior paint stabilization and porch repair. Genstone Field Services can handle ongoing preservation and inspections if the property will remain vacant during marketing. Lead paint is a concern in nearly every older Columbus REO, and exterior paint stabilization is planned with lead-safe practices in mind.

sections.h2: Renovating Columbus REO to the disposition plan
sections.body:
Not every bank-owned house should be renovated the same way. For a property headed to a retail buyer in Clintonville or Old North, a fuller rehab with updated kitchen and baths can maximize recovery. For a house in a lower-priced area that will sell to an investor, a lighter scope that addresses safety, systems and code issues is often the better choice. For a portfolio holding the asset as a rental, durability and tenant readiness drive the scope.

We write scopes to the disposition plan and, where useful, price more than one option so the asset manager can compare repair cost against projected value. For GSE and servicer clients, we follow the documentation, photo and bid requirements their programs call for, and our field manager stays in contact so the asset manager does not need to chase updates.

All work is done without upfront payment, draws are tied to completed and documented work, and final billing comes only after completion and approval.

faqs.q: Do you work with servicers and GSEs on Columbus REO properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Construction renovates bank-owned and REO properties for mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and we are a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We follow the bid, photo and documentation requirements those programs set and assign a field manager to each property. Asset managers see photos, milestones and draw requests without visiting the house, which matters when a portfolio is spread across Franklin County and beyond.

faqs.q: How do you handle freeze damage in a vacant Columbus house?
faqs.a: We start by walking and documenting the house, finding burst lines and water-damaged materials, and stopping any active leaks. Damaged plaster, drywall, insulation and flooring are removed and the structure is dried before mold remediation and rebuilding. Plumbing is pressure-tested before walls are closed, and a damaged furnace or water heater is evaluated for repair or replacement. Every step is photographed for the asset file.

faqs.q: Can Genstone maintain a Columbus REO property while it is being marketed?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services provides property preservation, inspections, code compliance and maintenance, so a renovated REO can be kept secure, clean and compliant while it is listed. That reduces the chance of vandalism, code violations or new damage undoing the renovation. Through the winter, that includes checking heat and winterization so a freshly renovated house does not suffer the same freeze damage that brought it to the servicer in the first place.
